title: Beyond Static Allocation: Dynamic Sensitivity-Aware Fine-Tuning for Vision Transformers
claim: Existing methods keep the same trainable modules fixed throughout training, whereas ours reconfigures which modules are active over time, as the brain does.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, brain graph inspiring a stacked static-vs-dynamic comparison
description: The left panel shows a gray network graph of nodes and edges. A few nodes glow blue or orange to represent sparse, dynamic brain activation. It is captioned "Brain's Sparse Dynamic Activation". A yellow "Inspire by" label and a blue arrow lead to the right panel, a rounded gray box. The box has two rows. The top row is "Static PEFT (Existing Methods)". It shows stacks of eight horizontal bars at "Early Stage" and "Late Stage", with an arrow between them. The orange (activated) bars sit in the same positions in both stages. The bottom row is "Dynamic PEFT (Our DAF)", separated by a dashed line. Its orange bars change position and number between stages. Blue bars are frozen modules, marked with a snowflake. Orange bars are activated modules, marked with a flame. A legend sits at the bottom right. The eye goes first to the colored bars and the glowing brain nodes.
caption: Inspired by the brain’s sparse and dynamic activation (Hill, 2025), the DAF framework periodically reconfigures its trainable structure. This contrasts with static PEFT methods that use fixed modules.
abstract: Existing Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods are fundamentally constrained by a static allocation paradigm, which overlooks the model's evolving optimization priorities during training. To address this, we introduce Dynamic Adaptive Fine-tuning (DAF), a novel framework that periodically evaluates and reconfigures the trainable structure based on a context-aware decoupled sensitivity analysis. DAF employs a Rebuild-and-Refocus strategy to preserve learned knowledge by freezing outdated modules while decisively reallocating the parameter budget to newly identified critical regions. Extensive experiments on challenging vision benchmarks demonstrate that DAF significantly outperforms mainstream static PEFT methods and achieves superior performance and efficiency, particularly under extreme parameter budgets. Our work fundamentally challenges the static nature of the field, offering a more intelligent and efficient paradigm for adapting large pretrained models. The code is available at https://github.com/E-green11/DAF.
